newsitem.title: UK: Dollar-friendly chorus lifts U.S. unit in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dollar-friendly chorus lifts U.S. unit in Europe.

text.p: An international chorus of dollar-friendly comments propelled the U.S. currency to probe back above 1.51 marks by late European trade.
Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer was the latest to add his voice, welcoming the dollar's recent rally and saying he "would not mind if it were to go a little further".

Earlier, influential Japanese official Eisuke Sakakibara said he welcomed currency market developments since April 1995. U.S. Treasury Undersecretary Jeffrey Shafer said Wednesday that U.S. exchange rate policy still favoured dollar strength.

"It's a concerted effort. I don't quite know why they need to talk the dollar up here, but they're certainly doing a successful job," said Alan Collins, head of technical analysis at Merita Bank in London.
The dollar pushed to a session high of 1.5117 marks and settled at 1.5081/86 by 1616 GMT, up from late Wednesday's European level of 1.5052/57.

But dollar/yen went the other way, dropping to a session low of 111.15/25. Traders said it was depressed by mark/yen's slip below key support at 73.85 to the day's low of 73.71/74. The two pairs ended at 111.36/46 and 73.99/4.02 respectively yesterday.
Traders said dollar/yen was also hit by a newspaper report that U.S. economist Fred Bergsten was being considered for a top post in the second term of the Clinton administration.

Bergsten's office had no comment on the report, which said the economist -- who served in the Treasury Department under President Jimmy Carter -- was being considered as a replacement for Laura Tyson as head of the National Economic Council.

In the early part of the first Clinton administration, Bergsten recommended dollar depreciation to close the U.S.-Japan trade gap. Talk of his return to public office spooked traders as it rekindled fears of a retreat from a strong-dollar policy.
"Until uncertainty over U.S. policy is removed, the dollar's going to remain vulnerable on the downside," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International in London.

The market has been concerned the G3 firm-dollar consensus might be unravelling since Sakakibara, director general of the Japanese Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, said last week that dollar/yen's correction was nearing an end.

But his comments today, including assertions that Group of Seven cooperation on currencies remains unchanged and that Japan's economy was neither strong nor weak, helped soothe those fears, analysts said.
"What he has done is implicitly say that (Japanese) interest rate policy is on hold as far as the eye can see, almost," said Adam Chester, senior analyst at Yamaichi International here.
U.S. data out today painted an inflation-benign picture, which analysts said backed the Federal Open Market Committee's decision to leave policy on hold after yesterday's meeting.

October consumer prices rose 0.3 percent on the month and 3.0 on the year, with core CPI up 0.2 percent and 2.6. The numbers matched economists' forecasts. Retail sales rose 0.2 percent, while weekly jobless claims fell more than expected to 328,000 from the a revised 332,000 in the previous week.
"The data confirm the U.S. economy is heading for a soft landing, inflation remains subdued and the Fed is going to sit on its hands for the time being," said DKB's Stamenkovic.
U.S. October industrial production and capacity utilization numbers out Friday should confirm that impression, he said.

Elsewhere, sterling powered to fresh four-year highs against the dollar and hit its best level against the mark since June 1994, as a leap in retail prices fueled speculation of monetary tightening. It stood at $1.6645/55 and 2.5123/34 at 1658 GMT compared to $1.6540/50 and 2.4903/13 in late Europe yesterday.
